title: The Many Ways of Being Heard
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece challenges the assumption that being heard in a meeting requires voicing an opinion, offering a list of subtler ways quieter or more reflective team members can register engagement. It cites tactics like asking clarifying questions, restating points for accuracy, and even nonverbal cues as legitimate ways to demonstrate presence. The article warns that team members who stay silent when they lack something substantive to add risk being seen as disengaged or uncommitted, regardless of intent. It offers a concrete benchmark — being heard every 10-15 minutes — for gauging engagement in a meeting.
points: Being heard in a meeting doesn't require advocating an opinion — many subtler options count.
Suggested tactics include clarifying questions, restating for accuracy, and even nonverbal cues.
Team members who stay silent risk being perceived as disengaged, regardless of their intent.
A rough benchmark of being heard every 10-15 minutes is offered for gauging engagement.
Reserved team members are urged to find their own way to register consistent presence.
quotes: Team members who play it safe by keeping their opinions about issues more closely guarded run the chance of not being heard and therefore not being seen as fully engaged in meetings.
Because many team members presume they must advocate or express an opinion to be heard, they sit silently when they don’t have anything special or substantive to say.
This short list is not exhaustive, nor will every tactic be appropriate in some meetings.
As a rule of thumb, a highly engaged team member should be heard every 10-15 minutes at a minimum.
Being heard is essential. The only question is when and how not if.
